# RBMK The AGCNR — the "RBMK" — is a gas-cooled nuclear reactor. Three pipes feed it: coolant in, moderator in, coolant out. Uranium fuel rods provide the neutrons, the moderator gas controls the reaction, and the coolant carries the heat away.
## Getting one The RBMK is sold by cargo as a flatpack, or printed from the engineering tech tree once researched. Use a multitool on the flatpack and wait for it to unfold. The site has to be bare plating across the whole 3x3, so pull up finished floor and clear primary-layer pipes, atmos devices, crates and tanks first; cables and off-layer pipes are fine. The flatpack lays its own reinforced footing, an HV cable across the footprint, and a pipe stub on each of the three ports, so the fitter only has to run services to the edge of the reactor. It does not arrive fuelled. A cold, shut-down RBMK built from a flatpack can be packed back into its flatpack from the context menu; a running, hot or slagged one cannot. Fuel rods are separate: each one is a 30 uranium, 10 metal print, or order a five-rod crate from cargo.
## The console - [bold]K (neutrons per generation):[/bold] the reactivity the control rods are chasing. 0–3. - [bold]Rod insertion:[/bold] the inverse of the K setpoint; 100 % is fully inserted. - [bold]Core temperature:[/bold] the number that decides meltdown. Power % is the core temperature against the 800 °C critical line. - [bold]Vessel integrity:[/bold] 400 points. The line under it names what is eating them. - [bold]Pressure:[/bold] the coolant outlet, in PSI. Over about 1470 PSI starts damaging the vessel. - [bold]Coolant in/out:[/bold] inlet and outlet temperatures. - [bold]Radiation:[/bold] the core's emission. - [bold]Fuel rods:[/bold] how many are loaded and how much fuel each has left.
## Starting it 1. Fill the coolant loop with a cold gas — oxygen, plasma or carbon dioxide — and turn the loop pumps on. Cold coolant in, hot coolant out. 2. Feed the moderator line. The classic mix is [bold]80 % oxygen / 20 % plasma[/bold]. Plasma is the fuel; oxygen multiplies the power. The gate burns everything in it every cycle, so the feed rate is the fuel bill: power scales with the gas, and opening a canister straight into the gate just drains it faster for watts you may not need. 3. Load the fuel rods. The pre-started reactor ships with five uranium rods; the exact count sets how much reactivity the control rods can push against. 4. Set K to 3 to start the reaction, then back to 1 when output reaches about 60 %. The rods chase the setpoint. 5. Vent or filter the nucleium that collects in the coolant outlet. It takes space and heat capacity from the loop.
## K and heat The reactor works in two-second cycles. Each cycle it adds the fuel rods' power and the moderator's fuel moles to K, and then the control rods pull K toward the setpoint by up to 0.65 per cycle; they cannot raise it faster than the fuel rods are producing neutrons. With fuel loaded, the core temperature rises by K each cycle; with no fuel, it falls by 10.
- [bold]K 0:[/bold] subcritical. The core cools. - [bold]K 1:[/bold] the normal running point. - [bold]K 3:[/bold] startup and high power. Watch the temperature.
More fuel rods raise the equilibrium K and the heat the core can make.
## Coolant and pressure The coolant inlet must hold at least 5 moles or the core is considered unfed. Cold inlet gas cools the core; warm inlet gas heats it. The outlet is forced to the core temperature, and its pressure is the vessel's pressure. Keep the outlet flowing to a radiator, turbine or space; if it backs up past about 1470 PSI, the vessel starts taking damage.
## Moderator gases - [bold]Plasma:[/bold] fuel. More plasma means more K and more power. - [bold]Tritium:[/bold] very hot fuel. Ten times the fuel value of plasma, and it raises radiation; use it carefully. - [bold]Oxygen:[/bold] power multiplier. A high-oxygen mix produces more watts from the same fuel. - [bold]Nitrogen / carbon dioxide:[/bold] control gases. They raise control-rod effectiveness, so the rods can pull K down faster. Both also raise radiation. - [bold]Water vapour:[/bold] permeability. It helps the coolant absorb heat from the core. - [bold]Nucleium:[/bold] waste. It is created as the core runs and should be filtered out of the coolant.
## Vessel integrity The vessel starts at 400 points and only goes down. The console's diagnosis line names the cause each cycle:
- [bold]Coolant starvation:[/bold] the inlet is below 5 moles for more than five cycles while fuel is loaded. The core starts eating itself; fix the coolant pump. - [bold]Over-temperature:[/bold] the core is above 900 °C. The damage scales with temperature; cool it or it will melt down. - [bold]Over-pressure:[/bold] the outlet is above about 1470 PSI. Vent it or the vessel will blow out.
When integrity reaches zero, the reactor either melts down (temperature) or blows out (pressure). Both leave a slagged core, a blast, and a radiation source. A slagged reactor cannot be restarted.
## Shutting down - Lower K to 0 and keep the coolant running. The rods will pull K down; once K is zero the core stops adding heat. - Do not pull the fuel rods while the core is hot; the console refuses above 20 % power. - If the reaction runs away, flood the moderator line with carbon dioxide or nitrogen. Both increase control-rod effectiveness; carbon dioxide is the stronger shutdown gas. - A slagged reactor is scrap. Do not plan on repairing one in the field.
## Tips - Keep the coolant inlet cold. The heat the coolant carries away is the power you get to use; a warm loop cools less. - Watch the vessel integrity line, not just the number. The line tells you whether to fix the pump, the temperature or the vent. - A number that looks stable this cycle can move a long way in ten seconds.
